new_statements.quote: Word stress is never lexically contrastive in Madurese, but we have the intuition that word stress in both disyllabic and trisyllabic words occurs in the first syllables. [...] Word stress for words with four syllables appears to fall on the antepenultimate syllable, for example, kabɤdɤʔɤn 'presence', kalɔpːaʔan 'forgotten' [...] (p.51) It appears that word stress in Madurese is neither dependent nor affected by vowel height. [...] even the first syllable of a disyllabic or trisyllabic word contains a schwa vowel, the stress remains on the first syllable [...] If we look at the word stress for words with more than three syllables, we see a fairly consistent and regular pattern that it always occurs in the first syllable of the root. (p.52)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not lexically contrastive. On the author's native-speaker intuition (explicitly not instrumental: 'To my knowledge, word stress is an area that has not been studied in Madurese.. The following description is based on my intuition as a native speaker', p.51), stress falls on the first syllable of disyllabic and trisyllabic words and on the antepenult of four-syllable words, which he unifies as stress on the first syllable of the root (bɤdɤ -> ka-bɤdɤʔ-ɤn, sapɔ -> a-sapɔ-an). Placement is insensitive to vowel quality: an initial-syllable schwa keeps the stress (pəlːɔ 'sweat', təlːɔʔ 'three'). Footnote 7 (p.49): in vowel clusters 'Impressionistically the first vowel in the cluster is stressed and longer.' The conclusions (p.209) restate that no phonetic study of Madurese word stress exists and that Indonesian and Betawi Malay 'have been suggested as stress-free languages', flagging the question as open.
new_statements.exceptions: No lexical exceptions given; the only qualifications are that the account is intuition-based and untested, that vowel height/schwa does not shift stress, and (p.39) that Sumenep (Eastern) speakers 'speak with a different intonation from Bangkalan people who speak Western Madurese', with no phonetic study of dialect prosody to date. Note one trisyllabic example, patəpːaʔ 'make correct' (prefixed pa-), is listed with first-syllable stress, which sits awkwardly with the root-initial generalisation; the author does not comment on it.
new_statements.identity_note: Misnadin does not describe a specific dialect ('we did not look at specific dialects', p.38; participants from several dialect areas); the stress remarks are his own native-speaker intuition (dialect of origin not stated in the section). He notes (p.39) that Eastern (Sumenep) and Western (Bangkalan) Madurese differ audibly in intonation, unstudied.

readall_conflicts: The one listed work, Misnadin 2016 (pp.51-52), gives a definite placement: non-contrastive stress on the first syllable of the root (word-initial in 2-3 syllable words, antepenult in 4-syllable affixed words), unaffected by schwa, but the author states this rests on his native-speaker intuition and that word stress 'has not been studied in Madurese' (repeated p.209, where he groups the question with Indonesian and Betawi Malay being 'suggested as stress-free languages'). The two descriptive sources already held by the project from the 9/16 check (not in this works list) point the other way: Davies 2010:51 (quoted in full in Kaufman & Himmelmann's submitted 'Suprasegmental phonology' ms) says word stress 'is not a salient feature of Madurese', that the intonation group is likely the lowest relevant unit, and that isolated words 'exhibit stress on almost any syllable in the root'; Stevens 1968:67 n.15 says stress location is 'largely, perhaps completely, predictable in terms of syntax and internal intonation'. So: root-initial by native intuition (Misnadin) versus no consistent word-level stress / phrase-level prominence (Davies, Stevens, and K&H who class Madurese with the 'stressless Java prototype'). No instrumental study resolves it.
